Name: The Sacrosanctity of the Roman Tribunes and the Threshold of Bodily Veto
RagShortTexts: The person of a Roman tribune of the plebs was protected by a law backed by the curse of the gods and was sacred and inviolable
A tribune shouted his veto and blocked with his own body a consul's exercise of public power or an order to levy troops
It was the focus of the contest between plebeians and patricians in the struggles over wartime levies and the Oppian Law
BaseText: The tribunes of the plebs (Tribuni Plebis) were the unique guardians of the common people in the Roman Republic. Under the sacred sworn law (Lex Sacrata) established by the early secession of the plebs to the Sacred Mount, the person of a tribune was 'sacrosanct' (Sacrosanctitas): anyone who dared to lay hands on a tribune or do him bodily harm was declared an outcast cursed by the gods (Homo Sacer), whom anyone could kill on the spot without legal punishment. The tribune had the supreme right of 'intercession' (Intercessio): as soon as he cried out 'I forbid' (Veto) and placed his own body across the threshold of the Senate house or before a consul's tribunal, any conscription order, financial appropriation, court sentence or even decree of the Senate had to stop on the spot. Over the long years of war, the tribunes became the central shield of the plebeians in resisting the forced imposition of heavy taxes and in protecting the rights of plebeian sons.

Variants.Content: The tribune's door stands open day and night to every oppressed plebeian! As soon as a tribune steps in front of a consul's chariot, even the haughtiest grandee must bow his head and hear the voice of the people!

At this critical moment, with Hannibal's army bearing down on us, some short-sighted tribunes have actually used their veto to hold up the army's march for the sake of exemptions for a few plebeians. This is nothing less than betrayal of the city's survival!

That an official can stop the orders of an entire legion merely through the curse of the gods and by standing there in person, such a constitutional myth is a miracle utterly unimaginable in the despotic monarchies of the eastern Mediterranean.
